title: Clustered event times can preserve a finite aftershock count table and its mean Omori curve
abstract: We constructed a random time intensity that keeps the exact mean Omori curve and the full joint count law at any finite set of forecast endpoints, including all independent magnitude thresholds and any shared productivity mixture. The usual conditional uniform-time test can still reject with probability tending to one as the count grows. We tested eight sample sizes and exact first-product endpoints from a published USGS aftershock study. In 20,000 synthetic families, a half-mass pulse over one tenth of each protected cell gave at least one Holm timing rejection in 98.95% of families, against 5.03% without pulses. Endpoint counts stayed identical path by path. This does not invalidate rejection of the full Poisson process. It shows that such rejection alone does not identify a wrong mean curve or wrong issued count probabilities. The pulses are a mathematical stress test, not a fitted physical mechanism or evidence that the actual USGS products are calibrated.

display.caption: Timing tests reject a clustered process whose mean rate and protected endpoint count laws remain unchanged. Counts and endpoints come from eight published USGS configurations; all event times are synthetic.
